slides.title: Firewalls

slides.title: Why Network Security Matters?
slides.body:
The CIA Triad
Modern networks carry sensitive data like banking details, medical records, passwords, and private messages
Network Security protects this data from being read, changed, or blocked by attackers
It mainly focuses on three core properties, called the CIA Triad

slides.title: Why Network Security Matters?
slides.body:
The CIA Triad
Confidentiality: Only authorised parties can read the data; achieved through encryption
Integrity: data is not altered during transmission; achieved through hashing and message authentication codes
Availability: authorised users can access the network and services when needed; achieved through redundancy, load balancing, and DoS protection

slides.title: Why Network Security Matters?
slides.body:
Passive attacks: Attacker silently observes traffic (e.g., packet sniffing). Hard to detect; prevented through encryption
Active attacks: Attacker modifies, injects, or blocks traffic (e.g., MITM, DoS). Easier to detect; harder to prevent
Categories of Network Threats

slides.title: Firewall
slides.body:
Introduction
A firewall is a network security device, hardware, software, or a combination, that sits between a trusted internal network and an untrusted external network (typically the internet)
It examines every packet that tries to enter or leave the network and permits or blocks it based on a configured set of rules

slides.title: Firewall
slides.body:
Importance
Why a firewall is needed?
The internet is open by default, any packet can theoretically reach any reachable device
Without filtering, a server could receive malicious traffic on every open port
A firewall enforces a security policy: which traffic is allowed, which is blocked, and under what conditions

slides.title: Firewall
slides.body:
Position in Network
A firewall is usually placed between the internal LAN and the internet, often with the gateway router.
Host-based firewalls can also run on individual devices for extra protection

slides.title: Network Segmentation
slides.body:
Two Domain Types
A network segment where two devices transmitting at the same time can cause a collision
Only one device can transmit at a time without corrupting data
Smaller collision domain = fewer collisions = better performance
Broken by: Switches and Routers (each port creates its own collision domain)
Not broken by: Hubs and Repeaters — all ports share one collision domain
Collision Domain:

slides.title: Network Segmentation
slides.body:
Two Domain Types 
A set of devices that receive each other’s broadcast frames
Broadcast frames are sent to MAC address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF and reach every device in the domain
Larger broadcast domain = more broadcast traffic = larger attack surface
Broken by: Routers and VLANs (Layer 3 or logical segmentation)
Not broken by: Hubs, Switches, or Bridges by default

slides.title: Proxy Server
slides.body:
Introduction
A proxy server is an intermediary that sits between a client and a server, forwarding requests on behalf of one or the other.

slides.title: Proxy Server
slides.body:
1. Forward Proxy
A Forward Proxy sits between the client and the public internet. The client’s request goes to the proxy first, and the proxy forwards it to the destination server. The destination server sees only the proxy’s IP address, never the client’s

slides.title: Forward Proxy
slides.body:
How A Forward Proxy Works?
The client is configured to send all outbound traffic through the proxy
01
02
03
04
The client sends a request (for example, an HTTP GET), it goes to the proxy
The proxy applies its rules: is the site allowed; is the content appropriate?
If allowed, the proxy fetches the content from the destination server using its own IP
05
The proxy returns the response to the client. The destination never sees the client

slides.title: Proxy Server
slides.body:
Reverse Proxy
A Reverse Proxy is the opposite,  it sits between the public internet and a set of backend servers. External clients connect to the reverse proxy, believing it is the server. The reverse proxy then routes the request to the appropriate backend server

slides.title: Reverse Proxy
slides.body:
How A Reverse Proxy Works?
The client makes a request to www.example.com, which actually points to the reverse proxy
01
02
03
04
The reverse proxy receives the request and decides which backend server should handle it
The chosen backend server processes the request and returns the response to the proxy
The proxy returns the response to the client. The client never knows the backend server’s IP

Introduction
A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates a secure, encrypted connection, called a tunnel, between a user’s device and a remote network across the public internet. It makes the user appear as if they are physically inside the remote network

slides.title: VPN - Virtual Private Network
slides.body:
Encapsulation and Encryption
Two key building blocks: Encapsulation and Encryption
Encapsulation alone hides the original packet inside another packet, but does not make it unreadable
Encryption scrambles the data so that even if intercepted, it cannot be understood
A VPN combines both, the original packet is encapsulated in a secure, encrypted wrapper

slides.title: IPsec
slides.body:
Introduction
IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is a suite of protocols that provides authentication, integrity, and confidentiality at the Network Layer
Unlike TLS (which secures application-layer traffic) or WPA (which secures wireless), IPsec secures every IP packet, regardless of the application above

slides.title: IPsec
slides.body:
Two Main Protocols
Authentication Header (AH):
Provides: Authentication and Integrity (no encryption)
Adds an AH header with a packet hash.The receiver checks this hash to verify the sender and ensure the packet was not changed.
Does not provide confidentiality, the data is still readable by anyone who intercepts it
IP protocol number: 51
1

slides.title: IPsec
slides.body:
Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP):
Provides: Authentication, Integrity, and Encryption (confidentiality)
Adds an ESP header and trailer; the payload is encrypted
Most commonly used IPsec protocol — covers all three security goals
IP protocol number: 50
2
Two Main Protocols

slides.title: IPsec
slides.body:
Two Operational Modes
Transport Mode:
Encrypts and authenticates only the payload of the IP packet
The original IP header is left unchanged, routing information remains visible
Used for end-to-end communication between two hosts (host-to-host)

slides.title: IPsec
slides.body:
Tunnel Mode:
Encrypts and authenticates the entire original IP packet (header plus payload)
A new outer IP header is added, the original packet is hidden inside
Used for site-to-site VPNs between routers or firewalls (gateway-to-gateway)
Two Operational Modes

slides.body: Two Operational Modes

slides.title: Key Exchange
slides.body:
Before IPsec can encrypt, both ends need a shared key
IKE handles key negotiation in two phases: Phase 1 sets up a secure channel; Phase 2 negotiates the actual IPsec keys
The result is a Security Association (SA) - the agreed parameters for the secure session
IKE (Internet Key Exchange)

slides.body: Introduction

slides.title: Network Attacks
slides.body:
Common DoS Attack Categories
SYN Flood
Attacker sends TCP SYN packets without completing the handshake; the server fills its connection table with half-open connections
UDP Flood
Attacker sends huge volumes of UDP packets; the server wastes CPU responding with ICMP “port unreachable” replies
ICMP Flood (Ping Flood)
Overwhelms the server with ping requests
Volume-based (Flood) Attacks: Overwhelm bandwidth or connection tables

slides.title: Network Attacks
slides.body:
Ping of Death
Sends a malformed or oversized ping packet; older systems crashed
Smurf Attack
Sends ICMP echo to a broadcast address with a spoofed source IP; the entire network replies to the victim
Protocol Attacks: Exploit weaknesses in protocol implementations
Common DoS Attack Categories

slides.body:
